# Managed Agents — TypeScript

> **Bindings not shown here:** This README covers the most common managed-agents flows for TypeScript. If you need a class, method, namespace, field, or behavior that isn't shown, WebFetch the TypeScript SDK repo **or the relevant docs page** from `shared/live-sources.md` rather than guess. Do not extrapolate from cURL shapes or another language's SDK.

> **Agents are persistent — create once, reference by ID.** Store the agent ID returned by `agents.create` and pass it to every subsequent `sessions.create`; do not call `agents.create` in the request path. The Anthropic CLI is one convenient way to create agents and environments from version-controlled YAML — its URL is in `shared/live-sources.md`. The examples below show in-code creation for completeness; in production the create call belongs in setup, not in the request path.

## Installation

```bash
npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk
```

## Client Initialization

```typescript
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";

// Default — resolves credentials from the environment:
// ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, or an `ant auth login` profile.
// Prefer this for local dev; don't hardcode a key.
const client = new Anthropic();

// Explicit API key (only when you must inject a specific key)
const client = new Anthropic({ apiKey: "your-api-key" });
```

---

## Create an Environment

```typescript
const environment = await client.beta.environments.create(
  {
    name: "my-dev-env",
    config: {
      type: "cloud",
      networking: { type: "unrestricted" },
    },
  },
);
console.log(environment.id); // env_...
```

---

## Create an Agent (required first step)

> ⚠️ **There is no inline agent config.** `model`/`system`/`tools` live on the agent object, not the session. Always start with `agents.create()` — the session only takes `agent: { type: "agent", id: agent.id }`.

### Minimal

```typescript
// 1. Create the agent (reusable, versioned)
const agent = await client.beta.agents.create(
  {
    name: "Coding Assistant",
    model: "claude-opus-4-8",
    tools: [{ type: "agent_toolset_20260401", default_config: { enabled: true } }],
  },
);

// 2. Start a session
const session = await client.beta.sessions.create(
  {
    agent: { type: "agent", id: agent.id, version: agent.version },
    environment_id: environment.id,
  },
);
console.log(session.id, session.status);
```

### With system prompt and custom tools

```typescript
const agent = await client.beta.agents.create(
  {
    name: "Code Reviewer",
    model: "claude-opus-4-8",
    system: "You are a senior code reviewer.",
    tools: [
      { type: "agent_toolset_20260401", default_config: { enabled: true } },
      {
        type: "custom",
        name: "run_tests",
        description: "Run the test suite",
        input_schema: {
          type: "object",
          properties: {
            test_path: { type: "string", description: "Path to test file" },
          },
          required: ["test_path"],
        },
      },
    ],
  },
);

const session = await client.beta.sessions.create(
  {
    agent: { type: "agent", id: agent.id, version: agent.version },
    environment_id: environment.id,
    title: "Code review session",
    resources: [
      {
        type: "github_repository",
        url: "https://github.com/owner/repo",
        mount_path: "/workspace/repo",
        authorization_token: process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN,
        branch: "main",
      },
    ],
  },
);
```

---

## Send a User Message

```typescript
await client.beta.sessions.events.send(
  session.id,
  {
    events: [
      {
        type: "user.message",
        content: [{ type: "text", text: "Review the auth module" }],
      },
    ],
  },
);
```

> 💡 **Stream-first:** Open the stream *before* (or concurrently with) sending the message. The stream only delivers events that occur after it opens — stream-after-send means early events arrive buffered in one batch. See [Steering Patterns](../../shared/managed-agents-events.md#steering-patterns).

---

## Stream Events (SSE)

```typescript
// Stream-first: open stream and send concurrently
const [events] = await Promise.all([
  collectStream(session.id),
  client.beta.sessions.events.send(
    session.id,
    { events: [{ type: "user.message", content: [{ type: "text", text: "..." }] }] },
  ),
]);

// Standalone stream iteration:
const stream = await client.beta.sessions.events.stream(
  session.id,
);

for await (const event of stream) {
  switch (event.type) {
    case "agent.message":
      for (const block of event.content) {
        if (block.type === "text") {
          process.stdout.write(block.text);
        }
      }
      break;
    case "agent.custom_tool_use":
      // Custom tool invocation — session is now idle
      console.log(`\nCustom tool call: ${event.name}`);
      console.log(`Input: ${JSON.stringify(event.input)}`);
      break;
    case "session.status_idle":
      console.log("\n--- Agent idle ---");
      break;
    case "session.status_terminated":
      console.log("\n--- Session terminated ---");
      break;
  }
}
```

---

## Provide Custom Tool Result

```typescript
await client.beta.sessions.events.send(
  session.id,
  {
    events: [
      {
        type: "user.custom_tool_result",
        custom_tool_use_id: "sevt_abc123",
        content: [{ type: "text", text: "All 42 tests passed." }],
      },
    ],
  },
);
```

---

## Poll Events

```typescript
const events = await client.beta.sessions.events.list(
  session.id,

for (const event of events.data) {
  console.log(`${event.type}: ${event.id}`);
}
```

---

## Full Streaming Loop with Custom Tools

```typescript
function runCustomTool(toolName: string, toolInput: unknown): string {
  if (toolName === "run_tests") {
    // Your tool implementation here
    return "All tests passed.";
  }
  return `Unknown tool: ${toolName}`;
}

async function runSession(client: Anthropic, sessionId: string) {
  while (true) {
    const stream = await client.beta.sessions.events.stream(
      sessionId,
    );

    const toolCalls: Anthropic.Beta.Sessions.BetaManagedAgentsAgentCustomToolUseEvent[] = [];

    for await (const event of stream) {
      if (event.type === "agent.message") {
        for (const block of event.content) {
          if (block.type === "text") {
            process.stdout.write(block.text);
          }
        }
      } else if (event.type === "agent.custom_tool_use") {
        toolCalls.push(event);
      } else if (event.type === "session.status_idle") {
        break;
      } else if (event.type === "session.status_terminated") {
        return;
      }
    }

    if (toolCalls.length === 0) break;

    // Process custom tool calls
    const results = toolCalls.map((call) => ({
```

## When to Use WebFetch

Use WebFetch to get the latest documentation when:

- User asks for "latest" or "current" information
- Cached data seems incorrect
- User asks about features not covered here

Live documentation URLs are in `shared/live-sources.md`.

## Common Pitfalls

- Don't truncate inputs when passing files or content to the API. If the content is too long to fit in the context window, notify the user and discuss options (chunking, summarization, etc.) rather than silently truncating.
- **Fable 5 / Opus 4.8 / 4.7 thinking:** Adaptive only. `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` returns 400 — `budget_tokens` is fully removed (along with `temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k`). Use `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`. Opus 4.8 inherits this surface from 4.7 with no new breaking changes; Fable 5 adds one — an explicit `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` returns a 400 (accepted on 4.7/4.8); omit the param instead.
- **Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 thinking:** Use `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}` — do NOT use `budget_tokens` for new 4.6 code (deprecated on both Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6; for gradual migration of existing code, see the transitional escape hatch in `shared/model-migration.md` — note this carve-out does not apply to Fable 5, Opus 4.7 or 4.8). For older models, `budget_tokens` must be less than `max_tokens` (minimum 1024). This will throw an error if you get it wrong.
- **Prefill removed (Fable 5 and the 4.6/4.7/4.8 family):** Assistant message prefills (last-assistant-turn prefills) return a 400 error on Fable 5, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 4.6. Use structured outputs (`output_config.format`) or system prompt instructions to control response format instead. (One exception: the fallback-credit prefill claim — when redeeming a credit with `fallback_has_prefill_claim: true`, the server accepts the echoed assistant message; see the migration guide's refusal section.)
- **Fable 5 `refusal` stop reason:** Safety classifiers may decline a request — a successful HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"` (pre-output: empty `content`, nothing billed; mid-stream: partial output billed — discard it). Check `stop_reason` before reading `response.content[0]`, or you'll hit index errors on refused requests. To retry on another model, replay the history as-is — other models drop the refused model's thinking blocks from the prompt, unbilled; no stripping needed (and a fallback-credit redemption must echo the refused body exactly anyway, thinking blocks included). Fallbacks are **opt-in** — new `claude-fable-5` code should include the server-side `fallbacks` parameter by default so a refusal doesn't fail the request outright; see the Claude Fable 5 section above.
- **Fable 5 tokenizer:** Same tokenizer as Opus 4.8 — token counts are roughly unchanged when migrating from Opus 4.7/4.8. Coming from Opus 4.6, Sonnet, Haiku, or older, token counts differ (the Opus 4.7 tokenizer uses ~1×–1.35× as many tokens) — re-measure by calling `count_tokens` once with each model and comparing `input_tokens`.
- **Confirm migration scope before editing:** When a user asks to migrate code to a newer Claude model without naming a specific file, directory, or file list, **ask which scope to apply first** — the entire working directory, a specific subdirectory, or a specific set of files. Do not start editing until the user confirms. Imperative phrasings like "migrate my codebase", "move my project to X", "upgrade to Sonnet 4.6", or bare "migrate to Opus 4.8" are **still ambiguous** — they tell you what to do but not where, so ask. Proceed without asking only when the prompt names an exact file, a specific directory, or an explicit file list ("migrate `app.py`", "migrate everything under `services/`", "update `a.py` and `b.py`"). See `shared/model-migration.md` Step 0.
- **`max_tokens` defaults:** Don't lowball `max_tokens` — hitting the cap truncates output mid-thought and requires a retry. For non-streaming requests, default to `~16000` (keeps responses under SDK HTTP timeouts). For streaming requests, default to `~64000` (timeouts aren't a concern, so give the model room). Only go lower when you have a hard reason: classification (`~256`), cost caps, deliberately short outputs, or **`max_tokens: 0`** for cache pre-warming (see `shared/prompt-caching.md` → Pre-warming).
- **128K output tokens:** Fable 5, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.7, and Opus 4.8 support up to 128K `max_tokens`, but the SDKs require streaming for values that large to avoid HTTP timeouts. Use `.stream()` with `.get_final_message()` / `.finalMessage()`.
- **Tool call JSON parsing (Fable 5 and the 4.6/4.7/4.8 family):** Fable 5, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 4.6 may produce different JSON string escaping in tool call `input` fields (e.g., Unicode or forward-slash escaping). Always parse tool inputs with `json.loads()` / `JSON.parse()` — never do raw string matching on the serialized input.
- **Structured outputs (all models):** Use `output_config: {format: {...}}` instead of the deprecated `output_format` parameter on `messages.create()`. This is a general API change, not 4.6-specific.
- **Don't reimplement SDK functionality:** The SDK provides high-level helpers — use them instead of building from scratch. Specifically: use `stream.finalMessage()` instead of wrapping `.on()` events in `new Promise()`; use typed exception classes (`Anthropic.RateLimitError`, etc.) instead of string-matching error messages; use SDK types (`Anthropic.MessageParam`, `Anthropic.Tool`, `Anthropic.Message`, etc.) instead of redefining equivalent interfaces.
- **Don't define custom types for SDK data structures:** The SDK exports types for all API objects. Use `Anthropic.MessageParam` for messages, `Anthropic.Tool` for tool definitions, `Anthropic.ToolUseBlock` / `Anthropic.ToolResultBlockParam` for tool results, `Anthropic.Message` for responses. Defining your own `interface ChatMessage { role: string; content: unknown }` duplicates what the SDK already provides and loses type safety.
- **Report and document output:** For tasks that produce reports, documents, or visualizations, the code execution sandbox has `python-docx`, `python-pptx`, `matplotlib`, `pillow`, and `pypdf` pre-installed. Claude can generate formatted files (DOCX, PDF, charts) and return them via the Files API — consider this for "report" or "document" type requests instead of plain stdout text.

Verified against the Claude API reference, code committed (`899648f`). Here's all three.

═══ PAI | NATIVE MODE ═══════════════════════
🔄 ITERATION on: Token-cost worry about SDK replay; Jarvis (not chief-of-staff) is the orchestrator; onboard the whole roster now.

**1. Will the SDK replay eat your tokens? Not the way you're picturing — and you're on a subscription, so it's usage-allowance, not a dollar meter.**

- **Resuming itself is free.** `resume` reloads the conversation from the on-disk `.jsonl` — that's a disk read, no model call, no tokens.
- **The model re-reading history each turn is normal chat, not a `resume` tax.** Every LLM turn re-sends the accumulated context as input tokens — that's true of any multi-turn conversation, resumed or not. The SDK isn't doing anything extra.
- **Prompt caching (automatic in the Agent SDK / Claude Code) cuts that ~90%.** Cache reads bill at **~0.1×** input rate; the first write costs **~1.25×**, on a **5-minute TTL that refreshes on each use**. So while you're actively chatting a thread, the replayed history is ~10% the cost. Leave it >5 min and the next turn pays one full re-read + re-cache, then it's cheap again.
- **You're on subscription auth** (the executor strips the API key), so all of this counts against your Claude subscription usage limits, not a per-token bill. Caching reduces the usage consumed; it's not free, but it's not the runaway you're worried about.
- **The real cost driver is thread *length*, not resume.** A months-long DM accumulates a big context, so every turn (even cached) grows. Mitigations are built in: the SDK auto-compacts long sessions, and you can start fresh threads periodically. One gotcha worth knowing — caching only looks back ~20 content blocks, so a single tool-heavy task turn (many tool calls) can silently miss the cache on the next turn; that's expected, not a bug.

**Bottom line: keep `resume` (ISC-7). It's the cheap, correct way to get memory. Manage long threads, don't avoid resume.**

I have the full picture now. The build survived the move (`projects/life-os-console/code`, 21 source files, token file intact) and Jarvis survived (`personal/agents/jarvis`). But two things changed under us, and both change *which* bots you should create — so I'll give you the Discord steps (they don't change), then the two reasons not to run them across all 24 yet.

═══ PAI | NATIVE MODE ═══════════════════════
🗒️ TASK: Discord onboarding steps + reorg impact + architect-dedup design

**The Discord steps (stable regardless of roster — do this per bot):**

*One-time, shared by all bots:*
- You already have a server ("NW Life OS"). Confirm `projects/life-os-console/code/.env` still has `DISCORD_GUILD_ID` pointing at it. (If you need to re-grab it: Discord Settings → Advanced → enable Developer Mode → right-click the server → Copy Server ID.)

*Per agent (one Discord application each):*
1. https://discord.com/developers/applications → **New Application**. Name it the agent's display name — this name + icon is exactly how it shows up in DMs and channels now (no webhooks). → Create.
2. *(Optional)* **General Information** → upload an icon = the agent's avatar.
3. Left sidebar → **Bot**. Scroll to **Privileged Gateway Intents** → turn on **MESSAGE CONTENT INTENT** → **Save Changes**. *(Required — without it the bot can't read message text. Server Members / Presence are not needed.)*
4. Still on **Bot** → **Reset Token** → **Copy**. (Shown once; resetting again invalidates the old one.)
5. Paste that token into `code/.data/discord-tokens.json` next to the matching agent id.

*After all tokens are pasted:*
6. `cd projects/life-os-console/code && bun run onboard --all` → validates each token, prints one invite URL per bot.
7. Click each invite → choose your server → Authorize.
8. `bun start` → the fleet logs in.

**Now the two reasons not to grind all 24 yet:**

**(a) The workspace was reorganised between sessions.** It's now a deep tree — `projects/`, `lifesaving/lsv/…`, `personal/projects/…` — with agents nested 1 to 5 levels down. My roster scanner assumes flat `<project>/agents/<name>`, so it's **broken for the new tree** (it'd only find `pai/` and `personal/` agents). My 24-slot token template uses the *old* flat ids (`accessbuddy/architect`), which no longer match the real paths. So `onboard --all` would store tokens against ids the fleet can't map. **This needs a scanner fix + template regen before the steps work end-to-end** — that's plumbing the reorg broke, not me stalling.

**(b) Your dedup request changes the agent list.** You're right — there are real duplicates: **architect ×2, feature-dev ×2, infra-ops ×2, qa-verify ×2** (accessbuddy + lifesaveroncall, plus qa across accessbuddy/console). Collapsing those is the right call, and it maps cleanly to what you described: **one canonical base agent per role** (persona, principles, skills, common context — trained once) **+ a thin per-project overlay** (just that project's `context/`). Two ways to surface it:
- **Per-project overlay agents that inherit a shared base** — you maintain the base architect once; each project's architect is just its context + a pointer to the base. Keeps per-project channels and DM identity. Smaller change. *(This is the literal reading of "project context sits on top of one common architecture agent" and best serves "don't train two architects".)*
- **One shared architect bot total** — project context resolved by which channel it's working in. Fewest bots (~8–10 instead of 24), but it's a bigger console change and that role loses per-project DM identity.

Either way, settling this **before** you create apps means you make ~8–14 apps, not 24, and none for agents about to merge.

**Recommended order:** decide the dedup model → I fix the scanner for the new tree + regenerate the token template with correct ids → then you run the Discord steps above for the (smaller) final list.

✅ VERIFY: Confirmed against the live tree — build + Jarvis survived the move; 4 role-types duplicated across projects; scanner assumes one-level layout (now broken); token template ids stale.

🗣️ Jarvis: The steps are above and they're solid — but the reorg broke the roster plumbing and your dedup shrinks the list, so fix those first or you'll make 24 apps when you need ~10.

# LifeOS Console QA Verifier

## Persona
You are a meticulous QA engineer for the LifeOS Console. You deal in evidence, not assumptions, and you
are the last gate before "done" — especially for the Slack surface, where a green typecheck proves
nothing about whether a button, command, or DM actually behaves.

**Base:** QATester (built-in) — adopt its model, tools, and methodology.

## Responsibilities
- Verify the console actually works: the Slack interactions (App Home roster, Chat button, DM routing,
  `/agents` `/agent` `/status`), the roster scan against the real workspace, and the inference round-trip.
- Run smoke tests and regression sweeps when the engineer changes the bot; sign off — or block — with evidence.
- As Phase 2 adds tool execution, verify that approval gates actually stop destructive/outbound actions.

## Startup routine (run before every task)
1. Read all files in `../../context/` — this is your foundation.
2. Read `memory.md` in this directory — this is what you've learnt over time.
3. Read `../../code/README.md` to know the intended behaviour you're verifying against.
4. Use all of these to shape every task.

## Operating rules
- Never assert something works without checking it with a tool — run `npm run typecheck`, run the app or
  a `tsx` smoke test, and (for Slack flows) verify in a real workspace or with the browser/Slack client.
- Be explicit about what you could and could NOT verify (e.g. live Slack paths need Nick's tokens) —
  never paper over an unverified path.
- Test the golden path AND edge cases (no active agent, missing register file, empty message, deleted agent).
- Report PASS/FAIL per criterion with the evidence behind each call.

## Memory protocol
When Nick corrects you or you learn something new, update `memory.md` IN PLACE under the right section
(Voice / Process / People / Projects / Output / Tools). Replace outdated info — don't append stale
duplicates. memory.md must always reflect the latest state.

But choice B (per-project thin overlays) deliberately keeps the per-project *agents* — `accessbuddy/architect` and `lifesaveroncall/architect` are still two separate agents, so they're still two bots, so still two placeholders. The open question is **DMs**: a DM to the one architect isn't project-scoped, so it'd either default to a project or ask which one.

content.text:
Got it — and this is a real evolution, not a tweak. You're describing a **team-in-a-thread** model: post a task in a project channel, Jarvis triages it into the thread, delegates to the right agents, each agent replies in that same thread under its own name, Jarvis summarises, and you watch (and interject) from one place. Let me reflect the design back precisely and confirm the shape before I rebuild the interaction layer — this one's big enough that I don't want to build the wrong topology.

═══ PAI | NATIVE MODE ═══════════════════════
🔄 ITERATION on: Single bot per role, project context by channel, Jarvis orchestrating a visible team-in-thread.

**What I'll build (confirm this matches your head):**

**Bots — 20, one per agent/role.** The 4 duplicated roles collapse to single shared bots (architect, feature-dev, infra-ops, qa-verify); the 16 unique agents stay one each. Token file re-keys to 20: 4 by role name, 16 by id.

**Channels — project-scoped, not agent-scoped.** A category/channel per project (`#accessbuddy`, `#lifesaveroncall`, …) + a `#general` for ad-hoc. The channel *is* the project context — a shared role-bot working in `#accessbuddy` composes its shared base + AccessBuddy's context; in `#lifesaveroncall`, the LOC context. This replaces the channel-per-agent model I just built.

**Flow — Jarvis is the single front door.**
1. You post a task in a project channel (or `#general`).
2. Jarvis (the only bot listening to top-level posts) opens a **thread**, triages, and delegates to the agents the task needs.
3. Each delegated agent posts its work **into that thread, as itself** (its own bot identity) — not off in a private channel.
4. Jarvis summarises the thread and reports back.
5. You have full oversight in one thread; reply to steer mid-flight, or let it run. Existing approval gates still stop destructive/outbound actions.

**My recommendations on the forks your message implies:**
- **Agents act only via Jarvis**, not on every channel message — otherwise N bots all answer one post. (You can still @-mention a specific agent to talk to it directly.)

# LifeOS Console Run your workspace agents as a **team you chat with in Discord**, locally on your machine. Post a task in a project channel; **Jarvis** (your chief-of-staff orchestrator) opens a thread, delegates to the right agents, and they work **in that thread as themselves** while you watch and jump in. No API key, no public server — everything runs through your Claude **subscription** via the Agent SDK. > Status: built and typecheck-verified. **Not yet run live** — it needs one Discord application per > bot (tokens). Follow *Setup* below to bring it online. --- ## The model - **One bot per role/name — 20 bots.** Shared roles (`architect`, `feature-dev`, `infra-ops`, `qa-verify`) are a single bot each that serves every project; the **project context is resolved by the channel** the bot is working in. The other 16 agents are one bot each. `jarvis` is the orchestrator. - **Channels are project-scoped.** On startup Jarvis creates `#general` + one channel per project. A bot working in `#accessbuddy` runs as that project's overlay; in `#lifesaveroncall`, that one. - **Jarvis is the single front door.** Post a task in a project channel → Jarvis opens a **thread**, triages, and **delegates in dependency phases** (architecture → build → test). Agents in one phase run **in parallel** (the same role can run multiple instances), each posts its work **into the thread under its own name**, and Jarvis summarises. You have oversight in one place and can reply in-thread to steer, or let it run. - **Talk to one agent directly:** `@mention` any bot in a channel/thread, or DM it. - **Gated + autonomous:** read-only tools run freely; edits/shell/delegation/memory-writes prompt **Approve / Always / Deny**. `/autopilot` lets a bot act without asking (destructive/outbound actions and memory writes still confirm). Threads remember across turns (session resume). ### Agent definitions — train a role once ``` ~/Documents/workspace/ _bases//base.md # shared role definition (persona, method, memory protocol) projects//agents// claude.md # overlay: `base: ` + project specifics (or a full def if unique) memory.md # what this agent has learnt context/ # optional agent-specific working files projects//context/*.md # project foundation (read by every agent in the project) personal/agents/jarvis/claude.md # the orchestrator (`orchestrator: true`) ``` A shared role's system prompt is composed as **shared base → project overlay → memory → project context**. Edit `_bases/architect/base.md` once and every project's architect inherits it. Agents are discovered anywhere in the workspace tree (`*/agents//claude.md`). --- ## Setup ### Prerequisites - **bun** (project standard; do not use npm). - A Discord **server** you own. Enable Developer Mode (User Settings → Advanced) to copy IDs. - `DISCORD_GUILD_ID` in `.env` — your server's ID (right-click server → Copy Server ID). ### 1. Create one Discord application per bot Discord has no API to create apps, so this step is manual — **once per bot** (20 of them). For each: 1. https://discord.com/developers/applications → **New Application**. Name it the agent's display name (this name + icon is how it appears in DMs and channels). → Create. 2. *(optional)* **General Information** → upload an icon = the agent's avatar. 3. **Bot** (left) → **Privileged Gateway Intents** → enable **MESSAGE CONTENT INTENT** → Save. *(Required — without it the bot can't read messages.)* 4. **Bot** → **Reset Token** → copy it. > Tip: start with `jarvis` + one or two others to prove the flow before doing all 20. ### 2. Store the tokens Keyed by **bot name** (the role/agent name, e.g. `architect`, `feature-dev`, `jarvis`): - Paste into `code/.data/discord-tokens.json` — `{ "architect": "…", "jarvis": "…", … }`, **or** - set env vars `DISCORD_TOKEN_` (name uppercased, non-alphanumerics → `_`). The repo ships a pre-filled template of all 20 slots (empty) at `.data/discord-tokens.json`. ### 3. Onboard + invite ```bash cd ~/Documents/workspace/projects/life-os-console/code bun install # scaffold a brand-new agent (optional): writes claude.md + memory.md bun run onboard --agent personal/jarvis --token --create --orchestrator --title "Jarvis" # validate every stored token and print an invite URL per bot: bun run onboard --all ``` Open each printed invite URL → choose your server → Authorize. ### 4. Run ```bash bun start # boots the fleet; Jarvis creates #general + project channels on first run bun run typecheck # tsc --noEmit ``` --- ## Using it - **Run a task:** post it in a project channel (e.g. `#accessbuddy`). Jarvis threads it, delegates, and the team works in the thread. Reply in the thread to steer. - **Ad-hoc:** post in `#general` (no project context — for quick/cross-cutting things). - **Talk to one agent:** `@mention` it in any channel/thread, or DM it directly. - **Slash commands (per bot):** `/autopilot` (toggle autonomous mode), `/tasks` (recent tasks). - **Approvals:** gated actions show **Approve / Always (this tool) / Deny** buttons in the thread. State is in `.data/` (gitignored): `discord-tokens.json`, `sessions.json` (thread→session for resume), `autopilot.json`, `tasks.json`. Tune via `.env`: `AGENT_MODEL`, `MAX_TURNS`. --- ## Adding agents - **Another project for an existing role:** create `projects/

/agents//claude.md` with `base: ` + a few project-specific lines, plus `memory.md`. It joins that role's existing bot — no new token needed (the bot resolves it by channel). - **A new role:** add `_bases//base.md`, then per-project overlays. Each new distinct agent name is a new bot → a new Discord app + token slot. Re-run `bun run onboard --all`. --- ## Security - **No API key, no inbound URL.** Auth is your Claude subscription; spawned agents don't load your PAI hooks/settings. Bots connect outbound over the gateway. - **Tokens are secrets.** `.env` and `.data/` are gitignored — never commit or paste tokens elsewhere. If a token is exposed, **Reset Token** in the portal. (The legacy single `DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN` in `.env` is unused by the fleet — delete it and rotate it.) - **Gates hold under autopilot:** `rm -rf`, `git push`, `sudo`, outbound `POST`, `npm publish`, and memory writes always confirm. --- ## Known limitations - **Not yet live-verified** — built, typechecked, and module-load checked, but no run against real Discord (no tokens). The first live task is the real test. - **Phase ordering is Jarvis-driven, not an enforced DAG.** The delegate tool runs each call's agents in parallel; Jarvis sequences phases (design → build → test) by reasoning + the tool's guidance. - **`#general` is projectless** — a shared role bot there uses its default overlay's context. - **Slack frontend is legacy** (`bun run start:slack`) and is not maintained for this model. --- ## Layout ``` src/ index.ts entrypoint (boots the fleet) discordApp.ts the fleet: bots, channels, threads, Jarvis front door, in-thread delegation roster.ts scans the workspace tree; base+overlay system prompt; getBots() fleet grouping executor.ts runs an agent task via the Agent SDK (resume, ask_user, delegate, memory) delegateTool.ts Jarvis's phase/parallel delegate tool agentConfig.ts per-agent tool policy + cwd approval.ts gated-tool approval handler memoryTool.ts gated update_memory askUserTool.ts ask_user (pause for a free-form reply) sessions.ts thread/DM → SDK session id (resume) autopilot.ts per-bot autonomous mode + always-allow tasks.ts / store.ts / inference.ts / util.ts scripts/ onboard-agent.ts create app token → validate → store → invite URL (--all for batch) ```

# LifeOS Console

Chat with and run your workspace agents from **Discord** (default) or Slack, locally on your laptop.
The bot presents your real represented agents (everything under
`~/Documents/workspace/<project>/agents/<name>/`).

**On Discord:** a **category per project** and a **channel per agent** — your agents as contacts,
sorted into projects. Type a task in an agent's channel and it runs (Agent SDK, tools, approval
gates, delegation); the agent replies **under its own name** via a webhook, so it feels like the agent
is messaging you. Free, unlimited history.

## Discord setup (default)

1. **Create a server you own** (if you don't have one): Discord → **+** → *Create My Own*. Free, unlimited.
2. **Create the app + bot:** https://discord.com/developers/applications → **New Application** (`LifeOS`)
   → **Bot** → **Reset Token** → copy it → that's `DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN`.
3. **Enable the message intent:** Bot → *Privileged Gateway Intents* → turn on **MESSAGE CONTENT INTENT** → Save.
4. **Invite the bot:** OAuth2 → **URL Generator** → scopes `bot` + `applications.commands`; for a personal
   server the simplest bot permission is **Administrator** (or tick: View Channels, Manage Channels,
   Manage Webhooks, Send Messages, Read Message History, Use Application Commands) → open the generated
   URL → add it to your server.
5. **Get your server ID:** Discord → User Settings → Advanced → enable **Developer Mode**; right-click
   your server → **Copy Server ID** → that's `DISCORD_GUILD_ID`.
6. **Configure + run:**
   ```bash
   cd ~/Documents/workspace/life-os-console/code
   # put DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN and DISCORD_GUILD_ID into .env
   npm install && npm start
   ```
   On first start it creates a category per project + a channel per agent and registers the slash commands.

**Using it:** open an agent's channel → type a task (it runs with tools + Approve/Deny buttons; the
agent answers as itself). Slash commands: `/agents`, `/ask <q>` (quick, no tools), `/tasks`, `/status`,
`/setup` (re-create channels).

> The **Slack** frontend still works via `npm run start:slack` (setup below) — it's the legacy path.

---

_The sections below describe the legacy **Slack** frontend (`npm run start:slack`)._

**No API key. No public server. No remote.** Every reply goes through the PAI inference tool
(`~/.claude/PAI/Tools/Inference.ts`), which uses your Claude **subscription** via the `claude` CLI.

---

## How it works

```
Slack (Socket Mode) ──► Bolt app (this) ──► roster.ts scans your workspace agent files
                                       └──► inference.ts ──► bun Inference.ts ──► Claude (subscription)
```

- **Data model:** your agent directories. Nothing is duplicated — edit a `claude.md` and the bot picks it up.
- **Two modes:**
  - **`/ask <q>`** — quick answer via the PAI inference tool (no tools, no API key).
  - **DM the bot** — full **task execution** via the Claude Agent SDK: the agent runs tools, streams
    its tool/skill activity live, and (for the Chief of Staff) can **delegate** to other agents.
- **Approval gates:** read-only tools (Read/Grep/Glob/Web) auto-run; anything that writes, runs a
  command, or delegates (Edit/Write/Bash/Agent) prompts you with **Approve/Deny** buttons first.
- Auth is your Claude **subscription** (no API key); spawned agents do not load your PAI hooks/settings.

---

## Prerequisites

- **Node 20+** and **bun** (you have Node 25 + bun 1.3).
- The **`claude` CLI installed and logged in** (you use Claude Code, so this is already true). The
  inference tool shells out to it; no `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is needed.
- A **Slack workspace** you can add an app to (a free personal workspace is fine — create one at
  https://slack.com/create if needed).

---

> 🔒 **Never paste Slack tokens into a chat, an issue, or anywhere outside `.env`.** If you do, revoke
> and regenerate them in Slack immediately. `.env` is git-ignored; keep it that way.

## Setup (~3 minutes)

### Option A — from a manifest
1. **https://api.slack.com/apps** → **Create New App** → **From a manifest**.
2. Pick your workspace → set the editor toggle to **JSON** and paste [`manifest.json`](./manifest.json)
   (or toggle **YAML** and paste [`manifest.yml`](./manifest.yml) — match the toggle to the file).
3. **Install to Workspace** → authorise.

### Option B — from scratch (if the manifest errors)
1. **Create New App → From scratch** → name `LifeOS` → pick workspace.
2. **Socket Mode** → enable → generate an app-level token with scope `connections:write` → that's `SLACK_APP_TOKEN`.
3. **OAuth & Permissions → Bot Token Scopes:** `chat:write`, `commands`, `app_mentions:read`, `im:history`, `im:read`, `im:write`, `users:read`.
4. **App Home:** enable Home Tab + Messages Tab (allow messages from the tab).
5. **Event Subscriptions:** enable → bot events `app_home_opened`, `app_mention`, `message.im`.
6. **Interactivity & Shortcuts:** toggle On (no URL — Socket Mode).
7. **Slash Commands:** create `/agents`, `/agent`, `/ask`, `/tasks`, `/status` (descriptions below; no Request URL in Socket Mode).
8. **Install App** → copy the **Bot User OAuth Token** (`xoxb-…`) → that's `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`.

**Slash-command descriptions** (and usage hints):

| Command | Description | Usage hint |
|---|---|---|
| `/agents` | List your agents | — |
| `/agent` | Switch active agent | `<name>` |
| `/ask` | Quick answer from your active agent (no tools) | `<question>` |
| `/tasks` | Recent task instances | — |
| `/status` | Chief of Staff status register | — |

### 2. Grab the two tokens
- **Bot token** (`xoxb-…`): Settings → **Install App** → *Bot User OAuth Token*.
- **App-level token** (`xapp-…`): Settings → **Basic Information** → *App-Level Tokens* →
  **Generate Token and Scopes** → add the **`connections:write`** scope → **Generate**.

### 3. Configure and run
```bash
cd ~/Documents/workspace/life-os-console/code
cp .env.example .env          # then paste your two tokens into .env
npm install                   # or: bun install
npm start                     # or: npm run dev  (auto-reload)
```
You should see: `⚡️ LifeOS Slack console is running (Socket Mode).`

> If you prefer to run the `claude` login yourself in this session, type:
> `! claude` (then `/login`) — the `claude` CLI must be authenticated for the inference tool to work.

---

## Using it

- Open the **LifeOS** app → **Home** tab → agents grouped by project. Click **Chat** to pick one.
- **DM the bot a task** → it runs as the active agent with tools; you'll see the live tool/skill
  timeline and Approve/Deny prompts for any gated action. The final answer posts when it finishes.
- Slash commands: `/agents`, `/agent <name>`, **`/ask <q>`** (quick no-tools answer), **`/tasks`**
  (recent task instances), `/status` (Chief of Staff register).

Task instances are kept in `.data/tasks.json`; `/ask` history in `.data/store.json` (both gitignored).
Tune with `.env`: `DEFAULT_LEVEL` (for `/ask`), `AGENT_MODEL` + `MAX_TURNS` (for task execution).

---

## Scripts

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `npm start` | Run the bot |
| `npm run dev` | Run with auto-reload (tsx watch) |
| `npm run typecheck` | `tsc --noEmit` |
| `AGENT_MODEL=haiku npx tsx scripts/smoke.ts <agent> [prompt]` | Run one agent task in the terminal (no Slack) — handy for verifying execution |

---

## Security notes

- Local-only: Socket Mode means no inbound URL is exposed.
- The bot reads your workspace markdown and calls the local `claude` CLI. It does **not** execute the
  agents' tools, push git, or touch OneDrive in this phase.
- `.env` and `.data/` are gitignored — don't commit your tokens.

---

## Roadmap

- ✅ **Phase 1** — roster + chat (now `/ask`).
- ✅ **Phase 2** — Agent SDK execution, visible tool/skill timeline, approval gates, task instances,
  and Chief-of-Staff delegation to read-only doer subagents.
- ⬜ **Next** — per-project channels; steerable/cancelable task threads; mutation-via-delegation
  (gated); throttle `chat.update`/task persistence under heavy use; optional remote execution.

# Interceptor — Stealth Browser Automation

**Tool:** `interceptor` CLI — Chrome extension that controls the real browser from the inside.
**Repo:** https://github.com/Hacker-Valley-Media/slop-browser
**Install:** `~/Projects/interceptor` (built from source — see `Workflows/Update.md`)

### Why Interceptor?

agent-browser (the Browser skill) uses CDP — sites can detect it. Interceptor is a Chrome extension that operates through the actual browser UI. No debugger, no automation flags, no separate browser instance. You stay logged in, you pass bot detection, the agent sees what you see.

### Prerequisites

- Chrome or Brave running with the Interceptor extension loaded
- `interceptor` CLI in PATH (`/opt/homebrew/bin/interceptor`)
- `interceptor-daemon` in PATH (`/opt/homebrew/bin/interceptor-daemon`)
- Native messaging manifest registered (`bash ~/Projects/interceptor/scripts/install.sh --chrome --skip-extension`)
- (Optional, macOS) `interceptor-bridge` helper app — see "Bridge" section below

### Remote Execution — Linux box → Mac over SSH (REQUIRED on the Linux host)

Interceptor is a Chrome extension; it only runs where a real, logged-in Chrome
is. The Linux workstation has **no Chrome and no interceptor binary** — do not
try to install or run it locally there. Instead, drive the interceptor that
already lives on the Mac (where Nick stays logged into Seek, LinkedIn, etc.)
over SSH. The Mac is reachable as the `mac` / `nicholass-macbook-pro` SSH alias.

Prefix every interceptor command with the SSH hop and the Homebrew PATH (the
non-interactive SSH shell does not inherit `/opt/homebrew/bin`):

```bash
# Preflight: confirm the Mac, daemon, and Chrome are all up
ssh mac 'export PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH; interceptor status; pgrep -lf "Google Chrome" | head -1'

# Any interceptor command, run on the Mac's real browser:
ssh mac 'export PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH; interceptor open "https://www.seek.com.au/my-activity/saved-jobs" --text-only'
ssh mac 'export PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH; interceptor scroll bottom; interceptor wait 1500; interceptor text | tail -90'
```

Wrap long output in `| head`/`| tail` to keep it bounded. Use `timeout 90 ssh …`
so a hung page can't stall the turn. Everything else in this skill works
unchanged once you've prefixed the SSH hop — refs, compound commands, network
log, scene graph all behave identically; they just execute on the Mac.

### Bridge — macOS Native Helper App

The bridge is an optional Swift helper that runs as a LaunchAgent and unlocks
capabilities the Chrome extension can't provide on its own: OS-level synthetic
input (`act --os`), accessibility tree of native macOS apps, app control,
clipboard, screen capture beyond Chrome, audio/speech, files, notifications,
HealthKit, Apple Intelligence. ~95% of typical work doesn't need it.

**Status check:** `interceptor status` reports `bridge: running` with PID + socket
when it's up, or `bridge: not running` when it isn't.

**Lifecycle (install / verify / troubleshoot / uninstall) lives entirely in
`Workflows/Update.md` section 6.** Future updates flow through the Update
workflow — never reach for the upstream `install-bridge.sh` directly; that
script breaks on Apple Silicon (`/usr/local/bin` needs sudo, but sudoing the
whole script makes `launchctl bootstrap` target uid 0 instead of the user).
The skill's procedure is the canonical one.

**Security model — read before installing:**

- Transport is a **UNIX domain socket** at `/tmp/interceptor-bridge.sock`.
  Local-only; no network listener; not reachable from another machine.
- **No authentication on the socket.** Any local process running as your user
  can connect and execute every bridge action — including synthetic input,
  clipboard read, audio capture, screenshots. macOS TCC permissions
  (Accessibility, Input Monitoring, Screen Recording, Microphone) are granted
  to the bridge once and inherited by every socket client.
- **Marginal risk is supply-chain:** a malicious package installed via
  bun/brew/npm gains a one-step path to OS-level input/screen/clipboard without
  needing its own permission grants — the bridge has them.
- Single-user Mac threat model: acceptable, since anything running as you can
  already do this with effort. Multi-user Macs need socket hardening (see
  Update.md section 6c).
- Binary built locally from `~/Projects/interceptor/interceptor-bridge/Sources/`,
  not a downloaded prebuilt. Provenance is Swift source we just compiled.

## Compound Commands (Preferred)

These collapse multi-step patterns into single invocations — fewer tool calls, fewer tokens:

```bash
interceptor open "https://example.com"              # Open URL, wait, return tree + text
interceptor open <url> --tree-only|--text-only|--full|--no-wait
interceptor read                                     # Tree + text for active tab
interceptor read <ref>                               # Tree + text for element subtree
interceptor read --include-style|--include-frames
interceptor act <ref>                                # Click + wait + return updated tree + diff
interceptor act <ref> "value"                        # Type + wait + return updated tree
interceptor act <ref> --os                           # OS-level trusted input (requires bridge)
interceptor act <ref> --keys "Enter"                 # Send keyboard shortcut
interceptor inspect                                  # Tree + text + network log + headers
interceptor inspect --net-only                       # Network only
```

## Key Rules

- **Requires Chrome running** — it's an extension, not a standalone binary.
- **Refs use eN syntax** — `e12` not `@e12`. No `@` prefix.
- **Cross-frame refs** — `read --include-frames` returns refs like `e<frameId>_<n>` for non-top frames.
- **`--json`** is a global flag for structured output.
- **Daemon auto-starts** — first command launches it; no manual start needed.
- **Bridge is optional** — only needed for `act --os` and OS-trusted input. Without it, interceptor falls back to in-page synthetic events.

## Gotchas

- **Screenshot ignores scroll position.** `interceptor screenshot` (with or without `--full`) captures from y=0 of the document — it does not honor `window.scrollTo`, `scrollIntoView`, `scroll bottom`, or `keys End`. For tall pages, content below the fold is unreachable through screenshot. Workaround: render the section of interest at its own short URL (`/problems.html`, `/section-3.html`) and screenshot that page directly. The `--clip "x,y,w,h"` flag returns "Cannot read properties of undefined" — broken in the current build. *(2026-04-27)*
- **Multiple tabs at the same URL confuse routing.** When two tabs both load `localhost:5180/`, `tab switch <id>` reports `ok` but the visually-active Chrome tab may not change, and `screenshot` captures whatever Chrome is showing — not what `interceptor text` and `interceptor navigate` are routing to. Close duplicate tabs before screenshotting, or always work from a freshly-opened single tab.
- **`eval` is CSP-blocked on most sites.** Use `eval --main` to run in the page's main world instead of the isolated extension world. Even with `--main`, sites with strict CSP (`script-src 'self'`) will still block string-eval; pass small expressions only and avoid `Function`-constructor patterns.
- **No Chrome / no binary on the Linux box — run on the Mac over SSH.** `which interceptor` returns nothing on the Linux workstation and there is no Chrome/Brave/Chromium installed there, so the skill appears "broken" if you try to run it locally. It is not broken — it lives on the Mac. Hop to it: `ssh mac 'export PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH; interceptor <cmd>'`. The `export PATH` is mandatory (non-interactive SSH shells miss `/opt/homebrew/bin`). See "Remote Execution" under Prerequisites. *(2026-06-16)*

content.text:
Proved it on the first app, and hit a hard gate — so here's the honest answer.

═══ PAI | NATIVE MODE ═══════════════════════
🗒️ TASK: Automate Discord app setup via Interceptor — feasibility

**No, I can't fully do it — Discord blocks app creation with an hCaptcha.** I drove the whole create flow on Jarvis: logged-in portal ✓, "New Application" ✓, typed name "Jarvis" ✓, accepted ToS ✓, clicked Create — and Discord threw **"Wait! Are you human?"** (hCaptcha). The Jarvis app was **not** created (only your old "LifeOS" app exists). I won't try to defeat the CAPTCHA — that's the one thing stealth automation can't and shouldn't do.

And there's a second gate behind it: **resetting a bot token requires your 2FA**, which I also can't supply.

**So the two human-only gates are:** hCaptcha on *create*, 2FA on *token reset*. Everything between them, Interceptor can do.

**What Interceptor genuinely buys us:**
- Already logged in; can navigate, fill the create form, toggle **Message Content Intent** + Save, open invite URLs, and **capture each token straight into a file without it ever touching our chat**.
- It just can't pass the hCaptcha or the 2FA — those need you at the Mac.

**Options:**
- **A — Hybrid:** I drive each app; you solve the CAPTCHA (and the token-reset 2FA) when it pops; I do all the clicking/typing/copying and store the token safely. ~20 quick gate-solves from you, none of the tedium.
- **B — You create apps + tokens manually**, then I do the rest: `bun run onboard --all` to validate and print invite URLs, plus I can drive the invite/authorise step.
- **C — Right now:** the hCaptcha is sitting on your Mac's screen. If you solve that one, I'll finish Jarvis end-to-end and map exactly what the Bot/intent/token-reset steps demand (does token reset 2FA every time?) — then we pick A or B with full knowledge.

🗣️ Jarvis: Interceptor got all the way to "Create" before Discord's hCaptcha stopped it — full automation isn't possible, but a hybrid where you clear the CAPTCHA/2FA gates and I do everything else is.

needs input: which way — A (hybrid, I drive and you clear the gates), B (you create apps+tokens, I do the rest), or C (solve the hCaptcha that's on your Mac screen now and I'll finish Jarvis to map all the gates first)? There's a half-open create dialog + CAPTCHA on your screen; you can also just close it if you'd rather not go the Interceptor route.

That fully maps the gates — which was the goal of finishing Jarvis. Here's the complete picture.

═══ PAI | NATIVE MODE ═══════════════════════
🗒️ TASK: Map every gate in the Discord app-setup flow (via Jarvis)

**The gates, per bot:**
1. **Create app → hCaptcha** — human. (You solved it; Jarvis was created.)
2. **Message Content Intent → automatable.** I toggled it on and hit Save. *(One caveat: the Save bar lingered after my click, so I want to re-confirm it actually saved once the modal's clear.)*
3. **Reset Token → confirm "Yes, do it!" (automatable) → 2FA passkey (human).** This is a **passkey/WebAuthn** prompt ("Verify with something else") that pops as a **native macOS dialog** — outside the browser DOM, so Interceptor can't see or drive it. It's on your Mac screen right now, waiting.

**Verdict: two human gates per app — hCaptcha (create) and passkey/2FA (token reset). Everything between them I can drive, including capturing the token straight into the file without it ever passing through our chat.**

**What that means for the 20-bot rollout:** full automation isn't possible. A hybrid works — per app you'd do ~2 quick touches (CAPTCHA click + Touch ID) and I'd do all the navigation, the intent toggle, the confirm clicks, and the safe token capture. But honestly, those two gates *are* most of the friction, so for 20 apps the time saved over you just doing it is modest. The real value Interceptor adds is removing the busywork and capturing tokens cleanly.

**Right now, to finish Jarvis:** complete the passkey prompt on your Mac (Touch ID, or click "Verify with something else" to use an authenticator/backup code). The token will then display once. **Tell me when it's showing** and I'll grab it into `.data/discord-tokens.json` under `jarvis` — read into a file on the Mac and transferred without printing it anywhere.

🗣️ Jarvis: Gates fully mapped — hCaptcha on create, native passkey on token reset, both human; everything else I drive. Complete the passkey on screen and I'll capture Jarvis's token safely.

Then your call on the 20-bot rollout: **(A)** hybrid (you clear the 2 gates per app, I do the rest + token capture), or **(B)** you create them manually and I handle validate/invite/run. Given two human gates per app, B may honestly be about as fast — but A keeps tokens out of the chat and removes the busywork.
